readings.head: {{RunningHeader|wonderfully|6963|woo}}
readings.c1s1:
¶
'''2.''' With wonder or admiration.
{{smaller block|Ther dide Gawein soche merveiles in armes that ''wondirfully'' was he be-helden of hem of logres, for he smote down men and horse.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 200.}}}}

'''wonderfulness''' (wun′dėr-fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being wonderful.

'''wondering''' (wun′dėr-ing), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wondring'', ''wundrunge'', < AS. ''wundrung'', verbal. n. of ''wundrian'', wonder: see ''wonder'', ''v.''] Expressing admiration or amazement; marveling.
{{smaller block|<poem>Swich ''wondring'' was ther on this hors of bras
That, sin the grete sege of Troye was,
Ther as men wondreden on an hors also,
Ne was ther swich a ''wondring'' as was tho.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Squire’s Tale, l. 297.}}}}

'''wonderingly''' (wun′dėr-ing-li), ''adv.'' In a wondering manner; with wonder: as, to gaze ''wonderingly''.

'''wonderland''' (wun′dėr-land), ''n.'' [< ''wonder'' + ''land''.] A land of wonders or marvels.
{{smaller block|Lo! Bruce in ''wonder-land'' is quite at home.
{{right|''Wolcot'' (''P. Pindar''), Complim. Epistle to James Bruce.}}}}

'''wonderly†''' (wun′dėr-li), ''a.'' [< ME. ''wonderly'', < AS. ''wundorlīc'' (= OS. ''wundarlīc'' = OHG. ''wuntarlīch'', MHG. G. ''wunderlich''); as ''wonder'' + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.] Wonderful.
{{smaller block|<poem>In his hed had on ey and no mo,
Moste hieste set, ''wonderly'' to se.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1241.}}}}

'''wonderly†''' (wun′dėr-li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''wonderly'', ''wondyrly'', ''wonderliche'', ''wunderlich'', ''wonderlyche''; < ''wonderly'', ''a.''] Wonderfully.
{{smaller block|''Wonderly'' delivere, and greet of strengthe.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol to C. T., l. 84.}}}}
readings.c1s2:
¶
{{smaller block|This towne of Modona is fayre and ''wonderly'' strong, as ferre as we myghte perceyue.
{{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 70.}}}}

'''wonder-maze†''' (wun′dėr-māz), ''v. t.'' To strike with wonder; astonish; amaze.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hee taught and sought Right’s ruines to repaire,
Sometimes with words that ''wonder-mazed'' men,
Sometimes with deedes that Angels did admire.</poem>
{{right|''Davies'', Wittes Pilgrimage, p. 51. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''wonderment''' (wun′dėr-ment), ''n.'' [< ''wonder'' + ''-ment.''] '''1.''' Surprise; astonishment.
{{smaller block|All this ''wonderment'' doth grow from a little oversight, in deeming that the subject wherein headship is to reside should be evermore some one person.
{{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, viii. 4.}}
“I know nothing o’ church. I’ve never been to church.” “No!” said Dolly, in a low tone of ''wonderment.''
{{right|''George Eliot'', Silas Marner, x.}}}}
'''2.''' Something wonderful; a wonderful appearance.
{{smaller block|Those things which I here set down are such as do naturally take the sense, and not respect petty ''wonderments.''
{{right|''Bacon'', Masques and Triumphs (ed. 1887).}}}}

'''wonder-net''' (wun′dėr-net), ''n.'' In ''anat.'', a term translating the Latin ''rete mirabile'', or wonderful net, a network of minute vessels. See ''rete.''

'''wonder-of-the-world''' (wun′dėr-ọv-thẹ̄-wėrld′), ''n.'' The Chinese ginseng: an alleged translation. See ''ginseng.''

'''wonderous†''' (wun′dėr-us), ''a.'' An obsolete form of ''wondrous.''

'''wonders†''', ''adv.'' [< ME. ''wonders'', < ''wonder'' + adv. gen. ''-s'' as in ''needs'', etc.] Wonderfully; wondrous.
{{smaller block|<poem>Me mette suche a swevenyng</poem>}}
readings.c2s2:
{{right|''Longfellow'', Flowers.}}

¶
'''wondrous''' (wun′drus), ''adv.'' [< ''wondrous'', ''a.''] In a wonderful or surprising degree; remarkably; exceedingly.
{{smaller block|I found you ''wondrous'' kind. ''Shak.'', All’s Well, v. 3. 311.

I shall grow ''wondrous'' melancholy if I stay long here without company.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Thierry and Theodoret, v. 1.}}}}

'''wondrously''' (wun′drus-li), ''adv.'' [< ''wondrous'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] In a strange or wonderful manner or degree.
{{smaller block|My lord leans ''wondrously'' to discontent.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., iii. 4. 71.}}
Cloe complains, and ''wond’rously'' ’s aggriev’d.
{{right|''Glanville'', Cloe.}}}}

'''wondrousness''' (wun′drus-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being wondrous.

'''wone†''', ''v.'' and ''n.'' See ''won''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wong'''<sup>1</sup> (wong), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wong'', ''wang'', < AS. ''wong'', ''wang'', a plain: see ''wang''<sup>1</sup>.] A plain; a field; a meadow. [Old and prov. Eng.]

'''wong'''<sup>2</sup>'''†''', ''n.'' An obsolete spelling of ''wang''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wonga-wonga''' (wong′gä-wong″gä), ''n.'' [Australian.] A large Australian pigeon, ''Leucosarcia picata'', having white flesh, and much esteemed for the table.—'''Wonga-wonga vine.''' {{smaller|See ''Tecoma.''}}

'''wonger†''', ''n.'' Same as ''wanger''.

'''woning†''', ''n.'' [< ME. ''wununge'', ''wuning'', ''woning'', ''woninge'', < AS. ''wunung'', dwelling, inner room of a dwelling (= OHG. ''wonunga'', G. ''wohnung'', dwelling), verbal n. of ''wunian'', dwell: see ''won''<sup>1</sup>.]
readings.c2s3:
Dwelling; abode.
{{smaller block|<poem>His ''woning'' was ful fair upon an heeth.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 606.}}
<poem>He signes unto them made
With him to wend unto his ''wonning'' neare.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. iv. 13.}}}}

¶
'''woning-place†''', ''n.'' [ME.; < ''woning'' + ''place.''] Dwelling-place; habitation.
{{smaller block|<poem>I wol and charge thee
To telle anon thy ''wonyng-places.''</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 6119.}}}}

'''woning-stead†''', ''n.'' [ME. ''wonnyng-steed; < woning + -stead.''] Dwelling-place.
{{smaller block|God will make in yowe haly than his ''wonnyng-steed.''
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 173.}}}}

'''wonne<sup>1</sup>†''', ''v.'' and ''n.'' See ''won''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wonne<sup>2</sup>†''', '''wonnen†'''. Obsolete forms of ''won''<sup>2</sup>, preterit and past participle of ''win''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wonne<sup>3</sup>†''', ''adv.'' and ''conj.'' An obsolete form of ''when.''

'''wont<sup>1</sup>''' (wunt), ''a.'' (orig. ''pp.''). [< ME. ''wont'', contracted form of ''woned'' (= G. ''gewohnt''), pp. of ''wonen'', be accustomed: see ''won''<sup>1</sup>.] Accustomed; in the habit; habituated; using or doing customarily.
{{smaller block|The Kyng of that Coutree was ''wont'' to ben so strong and so myghty that he helde Werre azenst Kyng Alisandre.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 164.}}
<poem>Our love was new and then but in the spring,
When I was ''wont'' to greet it with my lays.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, cii.}}}}

¶
'''wont<sup>1</sup>†.''' Obsolete preterit of ''won''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wont<sup>1</sup>''' (wunt), ''v.''; pret. ''wont'' (occasionally ''wonted''), pp. ''wont, wonted.'' [< ''wont''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'', orig.
readings.c3s3:
''vacillate, varicose'', etc.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To court; seek the favor, affection, or love of, especially with a view to marriage; solicit or seek in marriage.
{{smaller block|<poem>He ''woweth'' hire by meenes and brocage.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Miller’s Tale, l. 189.}}
<poem>She’s beautiful, and therefore to be ''woo’d;''
She is a woman, therefore to be won.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., v. 3. 78.}}}}
'''2.''' To solicit; sue; ask with importunity; seek to influence or persuade; invite; endeavor to prevail upon to do or to grant something.
{{smaller block|<poem>Having ''woo’d''
A villain to attempt it. ''Shak.'', Pericles, v. 1. 174.</poem>
<poem>I ''wooed'' her for to dine,
But could not get her.</poem>
{{right|''Phillada flouts me'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 310).}}
<poem>Thee, chauntress, oft, the woods among,
I ''woo'', to hear thy even-song.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Il Penseroso, l. 64.}}}}
'''3.''' To seek; seek to obtain or bring about; act as if seeking to obtain or bring about.
{{smaller block|Some in their actions do ''woo'' and affect honour and reputation. ''Bacon'', Honour and Reputation (ed. 1887).
<poem>Whose gently-looking beauties only do
Inamour Ruin and Destruction ''woo''.</poem>
{{right|''J. Beaumont'', Psyche, v. 6.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To court; make love; sue in love.

To court; seek the favor, affection, or love of, especially with a view to marriage; solicit or seek in marriage. {{smaller block|He ''woweth'' hire by meenes and brocage. {{right|''Chaucer'', Miller’s Tale, l. 189.}}}} {{smaller block|She’s beautiful, and therefore to be ''woo’d;'' She is a woman, therefore to be won. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., v. 3. 78.}}}} '''2.''' To solicit; sue; ask with importunity; seek to influence or persuade; invite; endeavor to prevail upon to do or to grant something. {{smaller block|Having ''woo’d'' A villain to attempt it. ''Shak.'', Pericles, v. 1. 174. I ''wooed'' her for to dine, But could not get her. {{right|''Phillada flouts me'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 310).}}}} {{smaller block|Thee, chauntress, oft, the woods among, I ''woo'', to hear thy even-song. {{right|''Milton'', Il Penseroso, l. 64.}}}} '''3.''' To seek; seek to obtain or bring about; act as if seeking to obtain or bring about. {{smaller block|Some in their actions do ''woo'' and affect honour and reputation. ''Bacon'', Honour and Reputation (ed. 1887). Whose gently-looking beauties only do Inamour Ruin and Destruction ''woo''. {{right|''J. Beaumont'', Psyche, v. 6.}}}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To court; make love; sue in love.
